summary: Specifies new socket options and functions for multicast source filters. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let receivers state which senders they will accept multicast traffic from, and this gives applications a programming interface to do so. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3678 describes socket interfaces that let a program choose which sources it accepts for a multicast group. It provides both small changes to a filter and functions that replace or retrieve the whole filter, while aiming to keep existing programs working.

questions: how to set source filters in igmpv3 programs
how do socket source filters work
what is the difference between include and exclude mode
subtitle: Socket options and functions for choosing which multicast sources a program accepts.

tldr.problem: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 support multicast source filtering, but applications need socket interfaces to request and inspect those filters.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IPv4-specific and protocol-independent socket options for changing a filter source by source, plus functions for setting or retrieving a complete filter.
tldr.outcome: The additions are designed to preserve compatibility with existing multicast programs. The RFC is Informational and says POSIX is the official sockets API specification.

today: RFC 3678 is an Informational RFC published in January 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC identifies POSIX as the official sockets API specification.

sections.title: Why Source Filters Need an API
sections.content:
The sockets interface is a widely used application interface for TCP/IP. IGMPv3 for IPv4 and MLDv2 for IPv6 allow receivers to express which multicast sources they want, but applications need socket options and functions to use those capabilities.

RFC 3678 defines those interfaces and the data structures passed to them. The RFC is Informational and notes that POSIX is the official standard specification of the sockets API.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast receivers can filter traffic by source, and programs need a standard way to request that filter. This RFC describes socket interfaces for those requests.

sections.title: Compatibility and API Choices
sections.content:
The additions are designed to preserve both source and binary compatibility with existing programs. They should require small changes for applications that add source filtering, and applications should be able to detect when the new interfaces are unavailable.

The RFC describes older ioctl() forms for historical purposes but prefers new functions for full-state operations. It says new functions provide type safety and can be implemented using an operating system's existing mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The new interfaces are intended to let old multicast programs keep working. A program can also check whether the new source-filter features are available.

sections.title: Changing One Source or the Whole Filter
sections.content:
The basic, or delta-based, API changes a filter one source at a time. In Any-Source Multicast, all sources are accepted by default and individual sources can be excluded. In Source-Specific Multicast, only listed sources are accepted.

The advanced, or full-state, API replaces a filter with a complete list of sources. Applications must use this API to switch between include and exclude modes without leaving a group. The RFC also recommends it for large source lists because one operation changes the filter atomically.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can add or remove one source at a time, or replace its complete source list in one operation. The whole-list method is needed to change filter modes while staying in the group.

sections.title: Basic Socket Options
sections.content:
IPv4 options include IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP and IP_DROP_MEMBERSHIP for joining and leaving an any-source group, plus IP_BLOCK_SOURCE and IP_UNBLOCK_SOURCE for blocking or restoring an individual source. Source-specific joins and leaves use IP_ADD_SOURCE_MEMBERSHIP and IP_DROP_SOURCE_MEMBERSHIP.

Protocol-independent options use group structures that can carry IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. The corresponding names include MCAST_JOIN_GROUP, MCAST_BLOCK_SOURCE, MCAST_JOIN_SOURCE_GROUP, and MCAST_LEAVE_GROUP. The RFC specifies errors for invalid addresses, invalid option use, unsupported retrieval with getsockopt(), and source limits.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic options let a program join or leave a group and block or unblock individual sources. IPv4-specific and protocol-independent forms are provided.

sections.title: Setting and Reading a Full Filter
sections.content:
For IPv4, the full-state functions are setipv4sourcefilter() and getipv4sourcefilter(). Protocol-independent versions are setsourcefilter() and getsourcefilter(). Each filter identifies a group, an interface, an include or exclude mode, and a source list.

When retrieving a filter, the source count supplied on input gives the size of the available list. On return, the count reports the total number of sources in the filter. If the list does not fit, an application can call again with a larger buffer.
sections.plainLanguage: The full-state functions set or retrieve an entire list of allowed or excluded sources. When reading a list, the returned count tells the program whether it needs a larger buffer.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content:
Source filtering can help against denial-of-service attacks, but it does not stop a sender from spoofing the address of an allowed source. The RFC notes that reverse-path forwarding in multicast routing provides some protection by dropping packets received on an interface other than the one toward the real source.

The RFC says this still does not guarantee protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A source filter can reject unwanted sources, but an attacker may imitate an allowed source address. The RFC says routing checks can help but do not guarantee protection.
